X.note: The 3D block-stack metaphor is dramatic. The tower dwarfs the 1950 block and the US slice, and the lighting and materials are good. But the US label sits low and is dim gray. The '1950' label has no value, so a viewer can't tell what it measures. The 4% fact is small and low-contrast. The footer source text is tiny on a phone. The tower runs off the top of the frame. The gridlines pass behind the tower, and the axis labels are far from the bars they refer to. The mix of 'one block = 100 Mt' and the Mt axis takes work to decode.

Y.note: This is a clean, bold two-bar chart with a large title and large values, so it reads instantly on a phone. It is a flat slide over a blurred background, with no depth or visual interest. The dashed 80% benchmark line runs through the '≈ 72%' and '≈ 77%' labels. The bars have no axis or zero baseline. The 72% bar overshoots its tick relative to the 77% bar, so the length scale looks slightly inconsistent. The footer source text is smallish.

why: Y delivers its single comparison (72% to 77% against an 80% benchmark) in about two seconds with large, high-contrast text, while X's more cinematic 3D scene has dim, small, ambiguous labels (the unlabeled 1950 block, the faint US callout) that slow understanding on a phone.
top_fix_for_weaker: Fix X's labels: give the 1950 block a value (e.g. '1950: 190 Mt' with the US share), make the U.S. 81.9 Mt callout bright and large with a clear leader line to the orange segment, put the axis labels next to the tower, and enlarge or drop the footer source text. Keep the 3D look but cut it to two or three big numbers.
